their amplified electrostatic coupling between divalent ions with higher charges and negative charges on the
nanotube walls, mediated by chargeI-dominant ion transport33,34. The light-gated ion flux regulation enables
programmable manipulation oRf multivalent ion transport dynamics, thereby establishing a versatile platform for
advanced optical-ion systems capable of supporting multiplexed signal encoding and multimodal
charge/information storage architectures.
Photosynaptic Function of the Nanofluidic Iontronic Device
Building upon the nanofluidic iontronic photoreceptor capabilities, we implemented synergistic optoelectrical
modulation to emulate photosynaptic behavior. A three-terminal ionic phototransistor was constructed,
consisting of a pair of Ag/AgCl electrodes immersed in two electrolyte reservoirs (Fig. 4a). This configuration
enabled simultaneous (i) external bias voltage application and (ii) monitoring of photoinduced ion currents
through the CNT/MoS nanotube under pulsed illumination. Different from photoreceptor characteristics, the
2
photoinduced ion currents exhibited persistent temporal response characteristics under 0.5 V bias potential,
similar to biological photosynaptic behavior (Fig. 4b-c). Meanwhile, the peak ion current demonstrated power
density-dependent gain from 1.5 to 6.1 µA under an illumination intensity range of 10-94 mW cm-2 (Fig. 4b),
and voltage-dependent gain from 1.0 to 15.7 µA over a bias voltage range of 0.1-0.9 V (Fig. 4c). In addition, the
CNT/MoS nanotube heterostructures and MoS nanotubes with reduced pore diameters of 35 nm exhibited
2 2
comparable optimal photocurrent modulation to their 90 nm pore-sized counterparts (Supplementary Fig. 18).
We systematically analyzed the relationship between excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) dynamics and
optical pulse stimulation in modulating short-term plasticity (STP) of the photosynaptic device. When stimulated
by two consecutive optical pulses at 0.1 V bias, the device exhibited paired-pulse facilitation (PPF), which is
recognized as a hallmark of short-term synaptic plasticity, with the second pulse generating significantly higher
EPSC amplitude (A ) than the first (A ) (Fig. 4d). The facilitation magnSitude was quantified by the PPF index =
2 1
(A − A ) / A × 100%, which follows a biexponential decay with increasing interpulse intervals17. This dynamic
2 1 1 R
behavior closely mimics the short-term plasticity characterisPtics observed in biological photosynaptic systems13
(Fig. 4e). Furthermore, long-term plasticity (LTP), whiNch converts transient photosynaptic events into persistent
memory traces through repeated activation, was e xperimentally modeled using sequential optical pulse trains35.
The spike-number-dependent plasticity eLmerges with increasing pulse counts (10 to 80), exhibiting both
progressive EPSC amplitude enhancement and prolonged decay kinetics (Fig. 4f).
The transition from STP to LTP can be mediated through pulse-duration optimization (spike-duration-
dependent photosynaptic Aplasticity) (Fig. 4g). Short optical pulses of 1 s induced rapid EPSC responses that
decayed to baseline. While prolonged optical stimulation from 1 to 20 s resulted in progressive augmentation of
EPSC amplitude with extended signal attenuation, signifying the LTP establishment. This transition mechanism
can be mechanistically attributed to optical stimulation-induced non-linear ion carrier accumulation. Meanwhile,
Fig. 4h systematically characterizes the pulse-frequency-dependent facilitation elicited by sequential
photostimulation across a physiological frequency range, which reveals a progressive enhancement of
incremental facilitation effects of EPSC amplitudes as the stimulation frequency increases from 0.05 to 1.00 Hz.
To emulate synaptic learning-memory functions, we implemented three consecutive training cycles of optical
pulse stimulation (Fig. 4i). Each protocol mimicked repetitive cognitive learning, demonstrating progressive
efficiency gains. The initial learning phase necessitated 40 training cycles to achieve full proficiency (100%),
followed by a reduced demand of 20 cycles in the second learning session, and further decreased to merely 10
cycles in the tertiary learning phase following an equivalent forgetting period. The progressive reduction in
training cycles across successive sessions demonstrates enhanced learning efficiency through periodic memory
consolidation, similar to biological memory consolidation processes36.
Applications of the Nanofluidic Iontronic Device
Orientation recognition represents a fundamental visual function essential for organizing complex
spatiotemporal information37,38. Notably, spatiotemporal correlation within the receptive fields of orientation-
selective ganglion cells enables the initial neural computation of movSing object trajectories39. Drawing
inspiration from orientation-selective ganglion cells, we developed a bioinspired orientation recognition system
based on our light-regulated nanofluidic iontronic device, impRlemented through an artificial neural network
(ANN) architecture (Fig. 5a). Here, three optoelectrically modulated nanofluidic devices were arranged at 120°
intervals on a circular platform, forming an orientation-sensitive detection array. The three devices, operated at
distinct bias voltages (Device#0.1V, Device#0E.3V, and Device#0.5V), exhibited characteristic EPSC response
profiles to angular illumination. This differential response enables reliable orientation recognition.
The dependence of EPSC on bias voltagIe and illumination power density was systematically investigated across
orientation angles. EPSC resRults exhibiting distinct synaptic weight modulation as a function of orientation
angles (Fig. 5b). Within polar coordinates spanning 0°-360° (in 30° increments), orientation-induced EPSC
demonstrated voltage-dependent amplification across a 0.1-0.5 V bias range (Fig. 5c). Furthermore, for any fixed
orientation angle, EPSC amplitude increased significantly with higher incident light intensity (Fig. 5d).
The synergistic integration of orientation-selective and illumination power density-dependent synaptic
weight modulation in artificial vision systems enables multidimensional control of imaging information. By
integrating our light-regulated nanofluidic iontronic device into an orientation-selective artificial vision system,
we demonstrate enhanced extraction of contrast and spatial resolution from landscape images captured across
multiple angles. Notably, images acquired at 90° exhibit superior contrast enhancement, confirming the
exceptional performance of our orientation-selective, light-controlled nanofluidic iontronic device for high-
resolution imaging applications (Fig. 5e). To identify complex spatiotemporal patterns, we developed a three-
layer artificial neural network (ANN) architecture capable of omnidirectional orientation recognition (Fig. 5a).
The input layer received flattened one-dimensional vectors representing the time-dependent currents from each
device. The network architecture also incorporated a hidden layer with 16 neurons and an output layer
comprising 12 neurons, corresponding to 12 distinct angular directions. To exploit the intrinsic memory
properties of the devices, we constructed a specialized training dataset comprising orientation-dependent EPSC
recordings over a 50-second post-illumination period. Remarkably, the model achieved a high recognition
accuracy of 98.5% after only 40 training epochs (Fig. 5e). In contrast, the instantaneous pattern recognition
system also achieves 98.8% recognition accuracy, together with response to light incident at various angles,
confirming the device exhibits strong robustness in complex pattern recognition capability (Supplementary Fig.
19). The confusion matrix for the test dataset demonstrates exceptional Sclassification accuracy across all angles,
with the majority of samples predicted correctly, as evidenced by the strong concentration along the matrix
diagonal (Fig. 5f). Moreover, the nanofluidic iontronic deviPce enables high-fidelity extraction and recognition
of complex visual features, such as fingerprint patternNs via convolutional neural networks (CNNs) employing
single fully connected hidden layer architectures for classification (Supplementary Fig. 20a). The 90° image
demonstrates optimal contrast and achieveLs the highest recognition accuracy, attaining 96.13% (Fig. 5g and
Supplementary Fig. 20b). The system maintained recognition accuracy (>95%) across multiple angles (0°–330°)
after 10 epochs, demonstrating high-fidelity feature extraction and reliable detection efficiency for practical
imaging applications (Fig. 5h and Supplementary Fig. 20c).

---

## Methods

Materials and Reagents
Acetonitrile (ACN) was purchased from J&K Scientific China. Ammonium tetrathiomolybdate ((NH ) MoS ),
4 2 4
sulfur powder (S), and dimethyl formamide (DMF) were purchEased from Aladdin, Shanghai, China. The
chemicals include LiCl, KCl, NaCl, MgCl ·6H O, and CaCl ·2H O were purchased from Aladdin, Shanghai,
2 2 P2 2
China. All aqueous solutions were prepared with Milli-Q w ater (18.25 MΩ·cm-1). The AAO membranes with a
thickness of 60 μm, and a pore size of ~50 nm and ~I100 nm were purchased from Puyuan Nano, China.
Fabrication of CNT
The CNTs were synthesized through a CVD equipment (BTF-1200 C-Ⅱ, AnHui BEQ Equipment Technology
Co., Ltd., China) employAing AAO membranes as nanostructured templates and ACN as the carbon feedstock.
The fabrication protocol was implemented in a horizontal tube furnace configured at atmospheric pressure. Prior
to growth initiation, the AAO substrate underwent thermal pretreatment at 1090 °C for 30 minutes under a
flowing gas mixture (Ar: 100 sccm, H : 50 sccm) to facilitate in situ reduction and surface activation. The CNT
2
growth was subsequently conducted by introducing ACN vapor through a carrier gas mixture stream at the
optimized synthesis temperature for 20 minutes. Post-synthesis cooling to ambient temperature was performed
under continuous argon purge (100 sccm) to prevent oxidative degradation, yielding vertically aligned CNT
arrays within the AAO template architecture.
Fabrication of MoS Nanotubes
2
The synthesis of MoS nanotubes was achieved through the AAO template-assisted CVD approach. Initially, a
2
precursor solution was prepared by dissolving 0.05 g of (NH ) MoS in 5 mL of DMF under continuous magnetic
4 2 4
stirring. The AAO templates were subjected to vacuum-assisted infiltration with the precursor solution, followed
by thermal treatment in a convection oven at 80 °C for complete solvent evaporation. Subsequently, the dried
AAO template was positioned in a quartz boat at the central heating zone of a horizontal tube furnace under
atmospheric pressure, while 0.2 g S was placed in a separate quartz boat 20 cm upstream from the furnace center
to prevent premature S evaporation prior to thermal processing. The system was rapidly ramped to 800 °C with
a mixed carrier gas (Ar: 100 sccm, H : 50 sccm) throughout the thermal treatment. Upon reaching the target
2
temperature, S powder moved quickly towards the tube furnace through an externally controlled magnetic
manipulation system that translated the sulfur-containing boat into the heating zone, which was maintained at
800 °C for 60 minutes to obtain MoS nanotubes.
2
Fabrication of CNT/MoS Nanotubes
2
The synthesis process of CNT/MoS
2
nanotubEe heterojunctions essentially combines the aforementioned two-
step fabrication methodology. Briefly stated, the pre-synthesized CNTs are initially impregnated with
(NH ) MoS precursor solution throuIgh vacuum-assisted filtration, followed by drying. Subsequently, the dried
4 2 4
CNT was positioned in a quaRrtz boat at the central heating zone of a horizontal tube furnace, while 0.2 g S was
placed in a separate quartz boat 20 cm upstream from the furnace center. The system was rapidly ramped to
800 °C with a mixed carrier gas (Ar: 100 sccm, H : 50 sccm). Upon reaching the target temperature, S powder
2
moved quickly towards the tube furnace, which was maintained at 800 °C for 60 minutes to obtain CNT/MoS
2
nanotube.
Fabrication and Measurement of Devices
The fabricated MoS and CNT/MoS nanotube heterostructure membrane-based devices were initially
2 2
encapsulated using a perforated polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) mold. Subsequently, these packaged devices
were mounted between a custom-designed electrochemical cell architecture with a fixed transparent area,
featuring dual symmetric reservoirs. Both compartments were filled with equal volumes of electrolyte solution.
Photogeneration was induced through lateral-side illumination using a xenon lamp or monochromatic laser
wavelength (365 nm, 405 nm, 520 nm, 590 nm, and 660 nm). A bipotentiostat configuration was implemented
using Ag/AgCl electrodes immersed in the reservoirs for transmembrane current signal acquisition. Photocurrent
was measured using a Keithley 2634 B (Keithley Instruments, Cleveland, OH).
KPFM Measurements
Surface photovoltage characterization was performed using a state-of-the-art KPFM integrated with an AFM
system (Bruker Dimension Icon). The measurements were carried out using Pt/Ir-coated silicon probes (Bruker
SCM-PIT series) with resonant frequencies between 60 and 100 kHz and spSring constants between 1 and 5 N·m-
1 in ambient conditions. To successfully reduce capacitive coupling artefacts between the probe and sample
surface, the amplitude-modulated KPFM technique was applieRd with optimal parameters: an AC modulation
voltage of 0.5 V and a dual-pass lift mode configuration using a minimum lift height of 20 nm. This configuration
achieved exceptional energy resolution (<5 mV) in mapping CPD variations. Photogeneration was induced
through front-side illumination using a xenon Elamp with different incident power densities.
Quantum-Mechanical Simulation oIf CNT/MoS Nanotubes
2
We systematically investigated the structural optimization and electronic excitation properties of CNT/MoS
2
nanotube heterostructures through advanced materials modeling techniques. First-principles calculations were
performed using the CP2K 2023.1 software package40 within the framework of DFT and TDDFT using the PBE
functional with empirical van der Waals correction by D3(BJ) scheme27. The CNT/MoS nanotube
2
heterostructures were constructed employing the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE) package. The
MoS /CNT composite model consists of a MoS nanotube and a CNT nanotube. Both the MoS nanotube and
2 2 2
the CNT nanotube were individually optimized under periodic boundary conditions. After constructing the
nested composite structure (Supplementary Fig. 6, using a supercell whose length along the z-axis corresponds
to the least common multiple of the minimal periodic units of both components), an additional geometry
optimization was performed for the combined system. Structural optimizations and electronic band structure
analyses were conducted using the PBE exchange-correlation functional, while long-range dispersion
interactions were accounted for through the DFT-D3(BJ) empirical correction scheme27. The electronic
wavefunctions were expanded using double-ζ DZVP-MOLOPT-SR basis sets in combination with Goedecker-
Teter-Hutter (GTH) norm-conserving pseudopotentials. Given the substantial unit cell dimensions of the
CNT/MoS nanotube heterostructures, Brillouin zone sampling was restricted to the Γ-point, with a plane-wave
2
cutoff energy of 400 eV employed to ensure computational accuracy while maintaining reasonable
computational efficiency. For post-processing analysis, electrostatic potential difference maps were generated
through a subtractive methodology using the Multiwfn 3.8 (dev) wavefunction analysis program41. Specifically,
the electrostatic potentials of isolated MoS and CNT fragments were subtracted from that of the coupled
2
CNT/MoS nanotube heterostructures to visualize interfacial charge redistribution. Furthermore, hole-electron
2
analysis was performed utilizing the same computational package to elSucidate the fundamental mechanisms of

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript reports a nanofluidic iontronic retina constructed from CNT/MoS₂ heterostructures, which integrates
photoreceptor-like optical sensing and photosynaptic functionalities within a single device platform through light-modulated
ion transport—a mechanism directly inspired by biological vision systems. The study is comprehensive, encompassing
sophisticated material synthesis, rigorous experimental characterization, and theoretical modeling, while also demonstrating
practical device-level applications such as orientation-selective recognition and fingerprint detection. The research
addresses a timely topic at the intersection of bioinspired neuromorphic computing, artificial vision, and nanofluidic
iontronics and represents a significant leap forward beyond conventional solid-state optoelectronic devices. The manuscript
is well-organized and supported by robust experimental and computational evidence. Nonetheless, several aspects require
clarification and further substantiation before publication. The detailed comments are outlined below.
1. In the introduction, the authors have compared and summarized the functional advantages of the work over currently
reported nanofluidic ionic devices and ionogel-based devices. In addition to these functional benefits, could the authors
further elaborate on whether their device exhibits advantages in terms of structural design, underlying mechanism, or key
performance parameters? A detailed comparative explanation would significantly strengthen the manuscript.
2. Throughout the manuscript, the authors consistently emphasize that the ion transport is driven by a photoelectric-effect-
induced potential, supported by various characterizations and simulation results. However, since carbon nanotubes exhibit
certain photothermal effects, how do the authors distinguish and demonstrate whether the ion transport is driven solely by
the photoelectric effect or by a synergistic effect of both photothermal and photoelectric mechanisms?
3. The manuscript does not address the operational stability or durability of the device under prolonged illumination. The
data would strengthen the case for practical applications.
4. In the section on material structure and surface property characterization, although the authors provide comprehensive
characterization data of the CNT/MoS₂ heterostructure nanotubes, many control experiments are missing. For instance, in
Figure S1d, only the morphological SEM image of the synthesized 35 nm pore-sized MoS₂ is provided, while the
morphology of the AAO template is absent. Additionally, Raman spectra of CNT and MoS₂ are missing in Figure S3. Please
provide the relevant supplementary data.
5. At the mechanistic level, the authors propose that unilateral illumination induces asymmetric potential-driven ion transport
via photogenerated electron-hole separation. To validate this mechanism, the authors should provide control experiments
under bilateral illumination to further verify the correctness of the proposed model.
6. Fig. 5 present neuromorphic computing for orientation recognition and fingerprint detection based on nanofluidic iontronic
retina; however, the implementation details are insufficiently described in the manuscript. The authors are expected to
provide a more detailed explanation.
7. In the section on neuromorphic computing, has this work completed the evaluation of the device's instantaneous pattern
recognition capability? Is the difference between memory-based pattern recognition and instantaneous pattern recognition
significant? Does the memory-based pattern recognition exhibit a sharp decline in accuracy?

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript entitled “Artificial Nanofluidic Iontronic Retina” presents a strategy for constructing light-regulated nanofluidic
iontronic device based on CNT/MoS₂ heterostructures, mimicking the retina with dual photoreceptor and photosynaptic
functions via light-modulated ion transport within a single device via bias-voltage-controlled modulation of photoresponse
dynamics. This iontronic device realizes accurate orientation recognition and robust fingerprint detection across a wide
range of incident light angles. Furthermore, the combination of theoretical (DFT, PNP) and experimental (KPFM, ion
transport measurements) offers a robust multiscale validation of the proposed mechanism. The manuscript is generally well
written and demonstrates considerable appeal and novelty, supported by a comprehensive dataset. The work is interesting
and potentially suitable for publication in Nature Communications after addressing the following concerns.
1 - In Figure 2, the authors performed first-principles density functional theory and finite element method simulations to
further validate the proposed mechanism. However, the authors provided only brief explanations of computational
procedures in the manuscript. Critical details, schematic illustrations of the simulation models, are lacking. It is
recommended that the authors supplement these to significantly strengthen the manuscript.
2 - In Figure 3, the authors modulate the ionic current by varying light intensity and wavelength as an ionic photoreceptor.
However, critical performance parameters of the photoreceptor, such as photoresponsivity ratio, response speed, and signal-
to-noise ratio, have not been quantitatively evaluated or provided. Please provide the relevant supplementary data.
3 - In Figure 3b, while the manuscript states that the ionic photoreceptor exhibits rapid rising and falling upon light
stimulation, its measured photoresponsive current still requires a considerably longer time to reach a steady plateau
compared to electronic devices. The authors should provide a clear explanation.
4 - In the manuscript, the authors have only characterized the photocurrent response resulting from light-induced ion
transport. In fact, the photo-driven ion transport can also generate a measurable photovoltage. Corresponding data should
be incorporated to further elucidate the underlying ion transport mechanism.
5 - In Figure S11, why is the photocurrent change minimal in both the CNT/ MoS2 heterostructure nanotube and the small-
pore MoS₂ nanotube when light and voltage stimuli are applied simultaneously? In contrast, as shown in Figure 3b, under
illumination alone, the CNT/ MoS2 heterostructure nanotube exhibits the optimal ion current generation compared to small-
pore MoS₂ nanotubes. A reasonable explanation for this apparent discrepancy should be provided.
6 - In Figure 5a, the schematic illustrating of orientation recognition lacks clarity in its annotations and comparative
visualizations. For instance, the difference in roof appearance between the 30° and 60° viewing angles is insufficiently
distinct. Additionally, the meaning of the symbol “I” in the input layer of the neural network? It is recommended that the figure
is modified to improve interpretability.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript reports the fabrication and characterization of a bioinspired nanofluidic iontronic device based on a carbon
nanotube/molybdenum disulfide (CNT/MoS₂) heterostructure, which is claimed to emulate both photoreceptor and
photosynaptic functionalities of a biological retina. The authors found that their device enables light-modulated ion transport
and photosynaptic behavior through heterointerface-induced photovoltage generation. Despite the appealing concept, there
are serious concerns with the manuscript as below
1) The claim of reproducing dual photoreceptor and photosynaptic functionality within a single nanofluidic device is
overstated. What is demonstrated are optical modulation of ionic currents and bias-dependent conductance changes, both
well established in prior optoionic memristor and photogated nanofluidic systems.
No convincing evidence is provided for actual retina-like spatiotemporal signal processing or for biologically relevant
timescales comparable to neural photosynapses. The “bioinspired retina” terminology reads more as rhetorical.
2) How do the memory curves look like, when they cycle the voltage, do the authors see pinched hysteresis loops, with or
without light? What is influenced by the light? Is it the area of the loop, low or high conductance state?
3) In Fig. 4c, the authors have shown the change in current as a function of bias voltage across the fluidic cell at a fixed
intensity of 94mW/cm^2. Why at 0.1V the change in current is of 1μA whereas in all subsequent measurements in the given
figure it is ~200nA?
4) Capacitive effects can also lead to the same changes as authors observed? How do authors know that it is not capacitive
effects due to light?
5) In Fig. 4d authors claimed short term plasticity behaviour and attempted to correlate it with Paired-pulse facilitation
characteristics. However, from figure it doesn’t seem trivial to assign it to short-term characteristics. Because, even when
both bias pulse/and photo-pulse were removed, the transient didn’t decay immediately back to the baseline.
6) In Fig. 4h, if authors are willing to demonstrate frequency dependent plasticity, they must show an increase and decrease
of post synaptic current as a function of frequency. To give an electrical analogy, a normal capacitor would exhibit a higher
current on increasing the frequency, but that doesn’t mean it exhibits spike frequency/rate dependent plasticity.
7) In supplementary Fig. S10, at 100mM KCl, why the system exhibited negative baseline? Is it normal for their model
system to observe?
8) Authors have performed zeta potential characterizations in supplementary figure S8. Although, these measurements do
show cation selectivity of their model system, however, it would be useful if they can perform drift diffusion type of
experiments at a fixed gradient as a function of light intensity. This would tell about which species in predominant in their
subsequently observed characteristics.
9) Key parameters that would enable meaningful comparison with state-of-the-art systems, response speed, energy
efficiency, stability, reproducibility, and endurance are not reported.
10) The ANN and CNN results depend primarily on preprocessed data, not on intrinsic device learning or neuromorphic
adaptability. These sections read as superficial add-ons applications, without clear connection to the nanofluidic
mechanism.
11) How do authors verify that the observed response is not simply due to the photoresponse of MoS2 rather than
nanofluidic mechanism.
12) The claim of “real-time operation” is not substantiated by explicit response-time measurements.
13) Several grammatical errors and typographical inconsistencies should be corrected.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Biological vision acquires externTal information through light-induced transmembrane ion transport, generating
electrical impulses. Emulating the dual visual functions of photoreceptors and photosynapses through light-
modulated ion transport presents a significant challenge. Herein, we present a bioinspired light-regulated
nanofluidic iontronic device that can mimic biological visual functionalities, realized through an engineered
carbon nanotube and molybdenum disulfide (CNT/MoS ) heterostructure. This bioinspired device combines two
2
key functionalities of photoreceptor-like optical sensing and photosynaptic signal processing with dynamically
adjustable polarity-switching behavior, achieved via bias voltage–modulated transient photoresponse speeds.
Both theoretical and experimental results prove that light-modulated ion transport originates from the
heterointerface-induced asymmetric photovoltage generation across CNT/MoS nanotube. Furthermore, we
2
demonstrate its implementation for both accurate orientation recognition and reliable fingerprint detection under
varying incident light angles. The device's bidirectional photoresponsiveness highlights its unique advantages
for adaptive visual simulation systems.

---

## Introduction

In biological systems, approximately 80% of external information is processed primarily through the visual
system1. The retina, a sophisticated neural tissue lining the posterior eye, serves as the gateway for visual
perception, owing to its anatomically integrated and intricately organized structure2 (Fig. 1a). Among these, the
photoreceptor cells and photosynaptic layers serve as the most critical components, with the former specializing
in light reception and the latter mediating information storage and interlayer communication3. Photoreceptor
cells rapidly capture light stimuli and convert them into electrical signals via photosensitive protein channel,
which precisely regulate ion transport, inducing membrane hyperpolarizaStion4 (Fig. 1b). The resulting light-
dependent electrical signals propagate via synaptic connections to downstream retinal neurons, enabling visual
information processing5 (Fig. 1c). Inspired by biological vision Rsystems, researchers have developed solid-state
optoelectronic devices that leverage semiconductor-based electron-hole separation mechanisms to emulate both
photoreceptor sensing and synaptic preprocessing functions6-11. However, the mechanisms behind how light
triggers localized interactions between electroEns, holes, and ions at interfaces are still not fully understood. This
gap in knowledge limits our ability to accurately mimic the ion-mediated signal transmission found in biological
visual systems, slowing the developmIent of advanced artificial photoreceptors and photosynaptic devices.
Over the past five years, Radvances in nanofluidic memristors have exploited nonlinear ion transport through
spatially confined systems in nano- and sub-nano channels and membranes to emulate biological synaptic
information processing, enabling brain-like computation through electrical-to-ionic and ionic-to-electrical signal
transduction mechanisms12-16. Meanwhile, recent advances in optically controlled ion transport based on ion-
conductive hydrogels and nanofluidic channel materials have partially achieved bioinspired visual
functionalities17,18. However, current research primarily focuses on biological photosynaptic functions, which
are limited by slow light-response speeds, thus failing to replicate the rapid detection of high-frequency visual
signals characteristic of photoreceptors. Given these limitations, creating a bioinspired visual system within a
single nanofluidic device that integrates photoreceptor-like optical sensing, photosynaptic processing, and
polarity-switching is still a major challenge.
Herein, we present a light-controlled nanofluidic iontronic device based on a carbon nanotube and
molybdenum disulfide (CNT/MoS ) heterostructure that emulates biological visual functions through a
2
sequential “light stimuli-electrical signal-electron/ion coupling-ionic signal” transduction process (Fig. 1d). This
platform achieves dual photoreceptor- and photosynaptic-like functionalities within a single device via bias-
voltage-controlled modulation of photoresponse dynamics. In a two-terminal model without bias voltage, the
device replicates photoreceptor cell operations with a rapid photocurrent responsive speed and responsive
specificity of light power density and wavelength. In a three-terminal configuration with bias voltage, the device
demonstrates photosynaptic characteristics including short-term plasticity, long-term plasticity, and experience-
dependent learning behaviors. The mechanism arises from the coupled effect between bias voltage and
photogenerated potential (E ) across the heterostructure nanotube (Fig. 1d), which together precisely control
photo S
ion transport across the CNT/MoS nanotube. This is facilitated by thSe one-dimensional coaxial architecture,
2
which establishes a continuous and enlarged heterointerface that not only enhances photogenerated charge
separation and strengthens the built-in electric field, but alsoP gives rise to a heterointerface-induced asymmetric
photovoltage. This photovoltage directly drives ioNn transport in a manner distinct from conventional
photothermal or surface-charge modulation sch emes19-21. The resulting ion photocurrent reaches 526 nA,
exceeding the performance of state-of-theL-art nanofluidic opto-ionic systems based on established material
platforms like metal organic framework (MOF)17, covalent organic frameworks (COFs)22, two-dimensional
transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes)19, and layered graphene oxide (GO)23,24. Furthermore, this
iontronic device realizes aAccurate orientation recognition and robust fingerprint detection across a wide range of
incident light angles, highlighting its potential for biointerfaced artificial retina.

---

## Results

Fabrication and Characterization of Nanotubes Heterostructure
The CNT/MoS nanotube heterostructure was fabricated via a two-step synthesis process. Initially, CNT was
2
synthesized using a porous anodic aluminum oxide (AAO) membrane template by chemical vapor deposition
(CVD). Subsequently, (NH ) MoS was thermally decomposed within the CNT to form MoS nanotubes.

Applications of the Nanofluidic Iontronic Device
Orientation recognition represents a fundamental visual function essential for organizing complex
spatiotemporal information37,38. Notably, spatiotemporal correlation within the receptive fields of orientation-
selective ganglion cells enables the initial neural computation of movSing object trajectories39. Drawing
inspiration from orientation-selective ganglion cells, we developed a bioinspired orientation recognition system
based on our light-regulated nanofluidic iontronic device, impRlemented through an artificial neural network
(ANN) architecture (Fig. 5a). Here, three optoelectrically modulated nanofluidic devices were arranged at 120°
intervals on a circular platform, forming an orientation-sensitive detection array. The three devices, operated at
distinct bias voltages (Device#0.1V, Device#0E.3V, and Device#0.5V), exhibited characteristic EPSC response
profiles to angular illumination. This differential response enables reliable orientation recognition.
The dependence of EPSC on bias voltagIe and illumination power density was systematically investigated across
orientation angles. EPSC resRults exhibiting distinct synaptic weight modulation as a function of orientation
angles (Fig. 5b). Within polar coordinates spanning 0°-360° (in 30° increments), orientation-induced EPSC
demonstrated voltage-dependent amplification across a 0.1-0.5 V bias range (Fig. 5c). Furthermore, for any fixed
orientation angle, EPSC amplitude increased significantly with higher incident light intensity (Fig. 5d).
The synergistic integration of orientation-selective and illumination power density-dependent synaptic
weight modulation in artificial vision systems enables multidimensional control of imaging information. By
integrating our light-regulated nanofluidic iontronic device into an orientation-selective artificial vision system,
we demonstrate enhanced extraction of contrast and spatial resolution from landscape images captured across
multiple angles. Notably, images acquired at 90° exhibit superior contrast enhancement, confirming the
exceptional performance of our orientation-selective, light-controlled nanofluidic iontronic device for high-
resolution imaging applications (Fig. 5e). To identify complex spatiotemporal patterns, we developed a three-
layer artificial neural network (ANN) architecture capable of omnidirectional orientation recognition (Fig. 5a).
The input layer received flattened one-dimensional vectors representing the time-dependent currents from each
device. The network architecture also incorporated a hidden layer with 16 neurons and an output layer
comprising 12 neurons, corresponding to 12 distinct angular directions. To exploit the intrinsic memory
properties of the devices, we constructed a specialized training dataset comprising orientation-dependent EPSC
recordings over a 50-second post-illumination period. Remarkably, the model achieved a high recognition
accuracy of 98.5% after only 40 training epochs (Fig. 5e). In contrast, the instantaneous pattern recognition
system also achieves 98.8% recognition accuracy, together with response to light incident at various angles,
confirming the device exhibits strong robustness in complex pattern recognition capability (Supplementary Fig.
19). The confusion matrix for the test dataset demonstrates exceptional Sclassification accuracy across all angles,
with the majority of samples predicted correctly, as evidenced by the strong concentration along the matrix
diagonal (Fig. 5f). Moreover, the nanofluidic iontronic deviPce enables high-fidelity extraction and recognition
of complex visual features, such as fingerprint patternNs via convolutional neural networks (CNNs) employing
single fully connected hidden layer architectures for classification (Supplementary Fig. 20a). The 90° image
demonstrates optimal contrast and achieveLs the highest recognition accuracy, attaining 96.13% (Fig. 5g and
Supplementary Fig. 20b). The system maintained recognition accuracy (>95%) across multiple angles (0°–330°)
after 10 epochs, demonstrating high-fidelity feature extraction and reliable detection efficiency for practical
imaging applications (Fig. 5h and Supplementary Fig. 20c).

The CNTs were synthesized through a CVD equipment (BTF-1200 C-Ⅱ, AnHui BEQ Equipment Technology

2

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript reports a nanofluidic iontronic retina constructed from CNT/MoS₂ heterostructures, which integrates
photoreceptor-like optical sensing and photosynaptic functionalities within a single device platform through light-modulated
ion transport—a mechanism directly inspired by biological vision systems. The study is comprehensive, encompassing
sophisticated material synthesis, rigorous experimental characterization, and theoretical modeling, while also demonstrating
practical device-level applications such as orientation-selective recognition and fingerprint detection. The research
addresses a timely topic at the intersection of bioinspired neuromorphic computing, artificial vision, and nanofluidic
iontronics and represents a significant leap forward beyond conventional solid-state optoelectronic devices. The manuscript
is well-organized and supported by robust experimental and computational evidence. Nonetheless, several aspects require
clarification and further substantiation before publication. The detailed comments are outlined below.
1. In the introduction, the authors have compared and summarized the functional advantages of the work over currently
reported nanofluidic ionic devices and ionogel-based devices. In addition to these functional benefits, could the authors
further elaborate on whether their device exhibits advantages in terms of structural design, underlying mechanism, or key
performance parameters? A detailed comparative explanation would significantly strengthen the manuscript.
2. Throughout the manuscript, the authors consistently emphasize that the ion transport is driven by a photoelectric-effect-
induced potential, supported by various characterizations and simulation results. However, since carbon nanotubes exhibit
certain photothermal effects, how do the authors distinguish and demonstrate whether the ion transport is driven solely by
the photoelectric effect or by a synergistic effect of both photothermal and photoelectric mechanisms?
3. The manuscript does not address the operational stability or durability of the device under prolonged illumination. The
data would strengthen the case for practical applications.
4. In the section on material structure and surface property characterization, although the authors provide comprehensive
characterization data of the CNT/MoS₂ heterostructure nanotubes, many control experiments are missing. For instance, in
Figure S1d, only the morphological SEM image of the synthesized 35 nm pore-sized MoS₂ is provided, while the
morphology of the AAO template is absent. Additionally, Raman spectra of CNT and MoS₂ are missing in Figure S3. Please
provide the relevant supplementary data.
5. At the mechanistic level, the authors propose that unilateral illumination induces asymmetric potential-driven ion transport
via photogenerated electron-hole separation. To validate this mechanism, the authors should provide control experiments
under bilateral illumination to further verify the correctness of the proposed model.
6. Fig. 5 present neuromorphic computing for orientation recognition and fingerprint detection based on nanofluidic iontronic
retina; however, the implementation details are insufficiently described in the manuscript. The authors are expected to
provide a more detailed explanation.
7. In the section on neuromorphic computing, has this work completed the evaluation of the device's instantaneous pattern
recognition capability? Is the difference between memory-based pattern recognition and instantaneous pattern recognition
significant? Does the memory-based pattern recognition exhibit a sharp decline in accuracy?

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript reports the fabrication and characterization of a bioinspired nanofluidic iontronic device based on a carbon
nanotube/molybdenum disulfide (CNT/MoS₂) heterostructure, which is claimed to emulate both photoreceptor and
photosynaptic functionalities of a biological retina. The authors found that their device enables light-modulated ion transport
and photosynaptic behavior through heterointerface-induced photovoltage generation. Despite the appealing concept, there
are serious concerns with the manuscript as below
1) The claim of reproducing dual photoreceptor and photosynaptic functionality within a single nanofluidic device is
overstated. What is demonstrated are optical modulation of ionic currents and bias-dependent conductance changes, both
well established in prior optoionic memristor and photogated nanofluidic systems.
No convincing evidence is provided for actual retina-like spatiotemporal signal processing or for biologically relevant
timescales comparable to neural photosynapses. The “bioinspired retina” terminology reads more as rhetorical.
2) How do the memory curves look like, when they cycle the voltage, do the authors see pinched hysteresis loops, with or
without light? What is influenced by the light? Is it the area of the loop, low or high conductance state?
3) In Fig. 4c, the authors have shown the change in current as a function of bias voltage across the fluidic cell at a fixed
intensity of 94mW/cm^2. Why at 0.1V the change in current is of 1μA whereas in all subsequent measurements in the given
figure it is ~200nA?
4) Capacitive effects can also lead to the same changes as authors observed? How do authors know that it is not capacitive
effects due to light?
5) In Fig. 4d authors claimed short term plasticity behaviour and attempted to correlate it with Paired-pulse facilitation
characteristics. However, from figure it doesn’t seem trivial to assign it to short-term characteristics. Because, even when
both bias pulse/and photo-pulse were removed, the transient didn’t decay immediately back to the baseline.
6) In Fig. 4h, if authors are willing to demonstrate frequency dependent plasticity, they must show an increase and decrease
of post synaptic current as a function of frequency. To give an electrical analogy, a normal capacitor would exhibit a higher
current on increasing the frequency, but that doesn’t mean it exhibits spike frequency/rate dependent plasticity.
7) In supplementary Fig. S10, at 100mM KCl, why the system exhibited negative baseline? Is it normal for their model
system to observe?
8) Authors have performed zeta potential characterizations in supplementary figure S8. Although, these measurements do
show cation selectivity of their model system, however, it would be useful if they can perform drift diffusion type of
experiments at a fixed gradient as a function of light intensity. This would tell about which species in predominant in their
subsequently observed characteristics.
9) Key parameters that would enable meaningful comparison with state-of-the-art systems, response speed, energy
efficiency, stability, reproducibility, and endurance are not reported.
10) The ANN and CNN results depend primarily on preprocessed data, not on intrinsic device learning or neuromorphic
adaptability. These sections read as superficial add-ons applications, without clear connection to the nanofluidic
mechanism.
11) How do authors verify that the observed response is not simply due to the photoresponse of MoS2 rather than
nanofluidic mechanism.

Orientation Recognition
In this study, the three-channel current data collected from the nanofluidic iontronic
devices was normalized and used to train an angle recognition by artificial neural
network. Each sample consists of three-channel current response signals extracted
within a specified sampling interval (covering a period with light application and/or
withdrawal). All samples were labeled according to their corresponding angle
categories (e.g., 0°, 30°, 60°, etc.), resulting in a total of 12 angular classes. The dataset
was split into training and test sets in an 80%:20% ratio, while maintaining class
balance during training. The constructed artificial neural network adopts a multilayer
perceptron (MLP) architecture: The input layer has a dimension of 885, corresponding
to the flattened three-channel current features; The hidden layer contains 16 neurons
utilizing the ReLU activation function; The output layer comprises 12 neurons
corresponding to the 12 angle classifications. The network was trained using the cross-
entropy loss function and the Adam optimizer (learning rate: 1×10-4) for a total of 40
epochs.
In the orientation recognition, we designed three nanofluidic iontronic devices
operating at different voltages, enabling them to exhibit orientation-dependent
photoresponses under varying incident light angles. Each incident direction produced a
unique set of photocurrent signals across the three sites, originating from the synergistic
light-electric-ion transport within the nanofluidic channels. These photocurrent signals
were directly fed into an ANN for learning and classifying the incident light directions.
Consequently, the ANN here functions not only as a standalone algorithm
demonstration but also as an analytical framework to interpret how device-level ion
dynamics and optoelectronic coupling mechanisms collectively enable orientation-
selective perception and neuromorphic-like sensory functions.
Fingerprint Recognition
This study constructed a convolutional neural network for 10-class classification (five
fingers from left and right hands) based on the SOCOFing fingerprint dataset. The
dataset includes real fingerprints and three difficulty levels of altered fingerprints
(Altered-Easy, Medium, Hard). During loading, finger type (thumb, index, middle, ring,
little) and hand information were parsed and mapped into 10 labels (0–9). All
fingerprint images were read in grayscale and uniformly resized to 96×96 pixels. They
were then split into training (80%) and validation (20%) sets, with the real fingerprints
used as an independent test set. The model employs a three-layer convolutional
architecture (kernel sizes: 5–5–3; corresponding channel numbers: 32, 64, 128). Each
convolutional layer is followed by Batch Normalization (BatchNorm), ReLU activation,
and 2×2 Max Pooling. After the feature extraction section, a Dropout layer was added
to prevent overfitting, followed by fully connected layers for classification output. The
model was trained using the Adam optimizer (learning rate: 1×10-4) and the cross-
entropy loss function for 10 epochs.The model was trained and evaluated using the
Sokoto Coventry Fingerprint Dataset, comprising 40,000 training images and 6,000 test
images (each 96×96 pixels in dimension), encompassing ten distinct fingerprint classes.
Training employed a batch size of 64 per epoch. The fingerprint images captured at five
distinct angular orientations following processing by the system.
In the fingerprint recognition, pixel values from an external image dataset were
converted into optical stimulation signals, which were directly applied to nanofluidic
iontronic devices. The light-induced ion transport processes within these devices
generated corresponding electrical signal outputs. These device-level current responses
reflect the nonlinear behavior of ion migration in the nanofluidic system and the
characteristics of light-induced conductance modulation. Subsequently, we employed a
CNN model to learn and extract features from these device output signals, aiming to
evaluate the capability of the nanofluidic system to perform data encoding and pattern
recognition in a neuromorphic context. Therefore, the neural network here serves not
merely as an independent algorithm demonstration, but also as an analytical tool to
quantify and interpret the dynamic response characteristics of the nanofluidic devices.

Response 3: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding the
photoresponse time of our ionic photoreceptor. The relatively slower response kinetics
are not a performance shortcoming but rather an intrinsic feature arising from the
different charge carriers involved. Our device operates on the principle of light-
modulated ion transport, in contrast to electronic devices that rely on the ultrafast
movement of electrons and holes. The explanation is as follows:
(1) Mass and mobility of charge carriers: The mass of ions (K⁺, Cl⁻) is several orders
of magnitude greater than that of electrons. Consequently, the mobility of ions in
aqueous solutions or nanochannels is drastically lower than electron mobility in
semiconductors. The finite time required for ions to physically migrate and redistribute
under the photogenerated electric field inherently leads to a slower current response.
(2) Interface-induced ion accumulation and concentration polarization: As detailed in
our manuscript (Fig. 2h and Supplementary Fig. 9), the operation of our CNT/MoS
2
heterostructure relies on the establishment of a photogenerated potential, which drives
ions and leads to significant concentration polarization at the heterointerface. This
process of building up a stable ionic concentration gradient is inherently slower than
the almost instantaneous separation of electron-hole pairs in a p-n junction.

discrepancy between the photocurrent changes in updated Supplementary Fig. 18 and
in Fig. 3b is not due to a contradiction but rather stems from a fundamental shift in the
dominant physical mechanism when the device operates in two-terminal (zero-bias)
versus three-terminal (applied-bias) configurations. The explanation is as follows:
In this two-terminal configuration (Fig. 3b), the ion current is driven solely by the
photogenerated potential arising from efficient band alignment-induced charge transfer
at the CNT/MoS heterointerface. This interfacial engineering strategy effectively
2
promotes spatial separation of photogenerated carriers through built-in potential
modulation. In contrast, single-phase MoS nanotubes exhibit suboptimal charge
2
separation efficiency and limited ion transport enhancement, primarily due to
insufficient band bending and homogeneous surface characteristics, despite improved
confinement effects achieved through pore size optimization. Overall, in this two-
terminal configuration, the photocurrent contribution originating from the
photogenerated potential-driven ion transport in the biphasic CNT/MoS heterojunction
2
nanotubes significantly outweighs that induced purely by nanoconfinement effects.
In this three-terminal configuration (updated Supplementary Fig. 18), the ion transport
is governed by the coupled effect of two electric fields: the external bias electric field
and the photogenerated potential. Although the coupled dual electric fields can
accelerate ion transport to generate a higher ionic current, the CNT/MoS
2

proportional increase in ion current induced by externally applied bias-driven ion
selectivity compared to nanotubes with small-pore (35 nm) MoS . Consequently, the
2

minimal. In contrast, for the small-pore MoS nanotube, its primary advantage is the
2
extremely strong spatial confinement effect. When both light and an external bias are
applied simultaneously, the external bias may accelerate selective ion transport within

photocurrent compared to that of the CNT/MoS heterostructure nanotube. Overall, in
2
this three-terminal configuration, the photocurrent contribution generated by bias-

potential-driven ion transport in the biphasic CNT/MoS heterojunction nanotubes.

Reviewer #3
General comments:
The manuscript reports the fabrication and characterization of a bioinspired
nanofluidic iontronic device based on a carbon nanotube/molybdenum disulfide
(CNT/MoS₂) heterostructure, which is claimed to emulate both photoreceptor and
photosynaptic functionalities of a biological retina. The authors found that their device
enables light-modulated ion transport and photosynaptic behavior through
heterointerface-induced photovoltage generation. Despite the appealing concept, there
are serious concerns with the manuscript as below.
Response: Thanks very much for your comments. We greatly appreciate your
evaluation and comments that are helpful for improving the quality of the manuscript.
We have revised the manuscript according to your suggestions point by point. The
revised parts are marked by red font.
Comment 1
The claim of reproducing dual photoreceptor and photosynaptic functionality within a
single nanofluidic device is overstated. What is demonstrated are optical modulation of
ionic currents and bias-dependent conductance changes, both well established in
prior optoionic memristor and photogated nanofluidic systems.
No convincing evidence is provided for actual retina-like spatiotemporal signal
processing or for biologically relevant timescales comparable to neural photosynapses.
The “bioinspired retina” terminology reads more as rhetorical.
Response 1: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that optical
modulation of ionic currents and bias-dependent conductance changes have been
individually demonstrated in prior optoionic systems, such as photogated nanochannels
and ionic memristors (Adv. Mater. 2025, 37 (30), 2502438; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025,
64 (7), e202418949; Nat. Commun. 2023, 14, 359; Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 4213; Adv.
Mater. 2025, 42, e08641). Here, we further demonstrate the coordinated regulation of
transient photoresponse speeds in ionic current (or conductance) within heterojunction
nanotubes at the single-device level through synergistic optoelectrical modulation.
In addition, the key advancement of our manuscript lies in the integrated and switchable
emulation of photoreceptors and photosynaptic dual functionalities within a single
device. As detailed in Figs. 3 & 4, in a two-terminal, zero-bias configuration, our device
exhibits a rapid photocurrent response, mimicking the fast transduction of
photoreceptor cells. Conversely, under a three-terminal configuration with an applied
bias, it demonstrates persistent photoconductivity with short/long-term plasticity,
emulating the slow, history-dependent processing of biological synapses. This voltage-
gated transition in photoresponse kinetics is a distinctive feature not reported in
previous systems. Previous works typically require separate device architectures or
material systems to achieve isolated photoreceptor or synaptic functions (Adv. Mater.
2025, 37 (30), 2502438; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64 (7), e202418949; Angew.
Chem. Int. Ed. 2019, 58, 12574–12579).
We acknowledge the reviewer's concern regarding terminology. It is true that we only
emulate partial functions of visual perception and signal processing, specifically those
of photoreceptors and photosynaptic functionality by modulating the fast and slow
components of ion currents, without fully replicating the complex functionalities of
retina. To prevent potential misunderstanding, in the revised manuscript, we have
replaced strong terms like "reproduce" with more accurate descriptors such as
"emulate" or "mimic." We have also toned down the claims surrounding "bioinspired
retina" and refocused the narrative on the demonstrated bioinspired functionalities
(i.e., co-mimicking photoreceptor and photosynaptic behaviors) rather than implying a full
replication of the entire retinal structure. The title of this manuscript “Artificial
Nanofluidic Iontronic Retina” has been corrected to “Bioinspired Nanofluidic Iontronic
Device with Integrated Photoreceptor and Photosynaptic Functions”
Comment 2
How do the memory curves look like, when they cycle the voltage, do the authors see
pinched hysteresis loops, with or without light? What is influenced by the light? Is it
the area of the loop, low or high conductance state?
Response 2: We thank the reviewer for this insightful question, which has prompted us
to further clarify the key memory characteristics and photomodulation mechanisms in
our nanofluidic iontronic device. In response, we performed voltage‑cycling
measurements using triangular wave sweeps to obtain the corresponding current–
voltage (I–V) characteristics. As illustrated in the accompanying figure, a well‑defined
pinched hysteresis loop, characterized by its “figure‑eight” shape that converges near
the origin, is clearly observed under both dark and illuminated conditions. Importantly,
illumination substantially enhances the overall ion current and device conductance.
Quantitatively, in the dark the area enclosed by the hysteresis loop is 1.36 mW, with
corresponding low‑ and high‑conductance states of 23.5 μS and 43.8 μS, respectively.
Under illumination, the loop area increases to 3.14 mW, while the conductance states
shift to 21.5 μS (low) and 51.2 μS (high). These changes indicate that light not only
enlarges the hysteretic memory window but also selectively elevates the
high‑conductance state, whereas the low‑conductance state undergoes a slight reduction.
Such behavior suggests that photoexcitation promotes ion migration and accumulation
within the CNT/MoS nanotube heterostructure, thereby enhancing the conductance
2
when the device is switched into the “on” state.
The observed light‑tunable pinched hysteresis represents a hallmark of ion‑based
memristive systems, which are capable of emulating synaptic plasticity. This
photomodulated memory effect aligns closely with photosynaptic functionality (Fig. 4),
wherein optical pulses can induce persistent conductance changes analogous to
spike‑timing‑dependent plasticity (STDP) in biological synapses. Consequently, this
dual electrical and optical tunability renders the device highly suitable for applications
in vision sensors and neuromorphic computing of orientation recognition and
fingerprint recognition (Fig. 5).
In summary, the clear emergence of a pinched hysteresis loop under voltage cycling,
and its pronounced amplification under illumination, underscores the role of
photogenerated potentials in governing ion transport and memory behavior. This
synergy between optical stimulation and ionic memristance is central to the device’s
ability to co‑emulate photoreceptor‑like sensing and photosynaptic processing within a
unified nanofluidic platform.

Comment 3
In Fig. 4c, the authors have shown the change in current as a function of bias voltage
across the fluidic cell at a fixed intensity of 94mW/cm^2. Why at 0.1V the change in
current is of 1μA whereas in all subsequent measurements in the given figure it is
~200nA?
Response 3: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful question. In fact, the apparent
discrepancy between the ~1 μA current observed at 0.1 V bias in Fig. 4c and the ~200
nA currents in subsequent figures (Fig. 4d-i) stems primarily from different testing
conditions. As stated in the manuscript, under identical applied bias voltage and
illumination power density, the generated photocurrent of the device is positively
correlated with the illumination duration of the optical pulse. The purpose of Fig. 4c
was conducted under 10-second optical pulse duration to establish a stable current-
voltage relationship. Under these conditions, charge carriers have sufficient time to
generate and accumulate, resulting in the larger measured current (~1 μA). In contrast,
for the subsequent photosynaptic characterizations (Fig. 4d-i), brief optical pulse
duration (2 seconds) was used to mimic biological synaptic responses to transient
stimuli. The shorter pulse duration limits the total number of photogenerated carriers;
hence the resulting transient current is smaller (~200 nA).
Comment 4
Capacitive effects can also lead to the same changes as authors observed? How do
authors know that it is not capacitive effects due to light?
Response 4: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the
potential contribution of capacitive effects. We understand that light-induced charge
rearrangement at the device interface could potentially trigger transient capacitive
effects. We have carefully considered this possibility and would like to clarify that the
observed phenomena are primarily attributed to the photoelectric effects at the
CNT/MoS₂ heterointerface, rather than purely capacitive effects. The key evidence is
outlined below:
(1) Distinct characteristics of surface photovoltage: Our KPFM measurements (Fig. 2d,
e) reveal a continuous and linear amplification of the contact potential difference and
surface photovoltage with increasing light intensity (from 3.8 mV at 0.1 mW cm-2 to
7.7 mV at 0.5 mW cm-2). This linear relationship is a hallmark of the photoelectric
effect, stemming from the continuous generation and separation of photo-induced
electron-hole pairs. In contrast, capacitive effects typically manifest as transient
charging/discharging current spikes and do not exhibit this sustained, linear correlation
with light power density.
(2) Theoretical evidence from first-principles calculations: Our DFT calculations (Fig.
2b, c) directly demonstrate spontaneous charge redistribution and the formation of a
built-in electric field at the CNT/MoS heterointerface. Furthermore, it shows clear
2
spatial separation of photogenerated electrons (localized on CNT) and holes (localized
on Mo atoms of MoS ) upon excitation. This provides a solid theoretical foundation for
2
the origin of the photogenerated potential, which is intrinsic to the photoelectric
mechanism and cannot be explained by capacitive effects.
(3) Ion transport behavior inconsistent with capacitive charging: The finite element
method simulations based on the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations (Fig. 2f-h) show the
generation of an asymmetric electric field and pronounced ion concentration
polarization (significant K⁺ enrichment at the illuminated interface) under unilateral
illumination. This spatially asymmetric and sustained redistribution of ions and
photocurrent is consistent with ion migration driven by a persistent photogenerated
potential, and is fundamentally different from the symmetric and transient characteristic
of capacitive double-layer charging/discharging.
(4) Experimental observation of long-timescale responses inconsistent with capacitive
charging: The characteristic timescale of capacitive responses is typically on the order
of milliseconds, with current decaying rapidly (Fig. R2b). In contrast, the photocurrent
we observed remains stable during illumination (Fig. 3b and R2a) and decays slowly
after light cessation, following ion diffusion and recombination kinetics, particularly
showing excitatory postsynaptic current relaxation under applied bias (Fig. 4). These
responses, lasting from seconds to tens of seconds, align with the migration,
accumulation, and release dynamics of ions in a nano-confined environment and cannot
be explained by conventional electric double-layer or interfacial capacitance models.
Fig. R2. Our Device-dominated vs. capacitance-dominated modulation of
photocurrent response kinetics. a, Our device-governed photoresponse speed
variation in current; b, Interfacial-capacitance-governed photoresponse speed variation
in current.
(5) Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy ruling out dominant capacitive
contribution: We performed electrochemical impedance spectroscopy measurements to
ob measurements to
obtain the Nyquist plot and Bode phase angle plot characteristics. If the photo-
responsive ion transport in our device were dominated by capacitive effects, the Nyquist
plot shows a straight line lies in y-axis (the real impedance is zero). Values close to
zero corresponds to high frequencies, while at lower frequencies the impedance values
are higher. The Bode phase angle plot shows a straight line that crosses the right axis
at φ = −90° based on the previous reported work (ACS Meas. Sci. Au 2023, 3, 162−193).
In contrast, the Nyquist plot we tested shows the majority of point lying in the real axis.
That is, the impedance values at all the excitation frequencies does not change
significantly in the dark or light illumination condition. The Bode phase angle plot
shows a straight line that crosses the right axis at φ = 0-5°, which equal to the resistance
characteristics. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy measurements were
conducted to further rule out a capacitance-dominated mechanism in the photo-
responsive ion transport.

In summary, the combination of SPV measurement, theoretical modeling, and control
experiments collectively confirms that the modulation of photoresponsive ion current
is predominantly governed by the photoelectric effects at the CNT/MoS

Comment 6
In Fig. 4h, if authors are willing to demonstrate frequency dependent plasticity, they
must show an increase and decrease of post synaptic current as a function of frequency.
To give an electrical analogy, a normal capacitor would exhibit a higher current on
increasing the frequency, but that doesn’t mean it exhibits spike frequency/rate

Response 6: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and important comment
regarding the interpretation of frequency-dependent plasticity. We fully acknowledge
the reviewer’s point that a purely capacitive system would exhibit a linear increase in
current with frequency. This stands in fundamental contrast to biological spike-
frequency-dependent plasticity, which is characterized by nonlinear, history-dependent
modulation of synaptic efficacy.
(1) In fact, as the frequency increases, particularly at the high frequency of 1 Hz, the
amplification of the observed postsynaptic current exhibits a distinct saturation trend.
This behavior clearly differentiates it from the linear current increase characteristic of
a capacitive system. Moreover, as demonstrated in Response 4, the photoresponsive
current in our nanofluidic iontronic system is attributed to light-induced asymmetric
potential-driven ion transport, rather than capacitive effects.
(2) In our experiments, the observed increase in EPSC amplitude with increasing
stimulation frequency (0.05–1 Hz) is not simply due to capacitive charging, but reflects
a cumulative facilitation of ion transport that is sustained beyond the stimulus period.
This behavior arises from the interplay between light-induced ion accumulation and the
finite relaxation time of ions within the confined nanotube heterostructure. At higher
frequencies, the inter-pulse interval is shorter than the ion redistribution time, leading
to progressive accumulation of ions at the illuminated heterointerface, thereby
enhancing the EPSC amplitude in a manner analogous to short-term facilitation in
biological synapses. To further distinguish our device’s response from that of a
capacitor, we performed additional analysis of the EPSC decay kinetics after each light
pulse train. As shown in the Fig. 4h, after high-frequency stimulation, the current does
not immediately return to baseline but decays with a time constant that depends on the
prior stimulation history, indicating a “memory” of the preceding activity. This post-
tetanic potentiation-like behavior is a hallmark of frequency-dependent plasticity and
cannot be explained by a simple capacitance circuit model.
To make this distinction explicit, we have revised the manuscript in Section
“Photosynaptic Characteristics” to explicitly describe the observed behavior as “pulse-
frequency-dependent facilitation”. We appreciate the reviewer’s critical comment,
which has helped us to more precisely characterize and explain the synaptic-like
dynamics of our device.

frequency-dependent facilitation elicited by sequential photostimulation across a
physiological frequency range, which reveals a progressive enhancement of
incremental facilitation effects of EPSC amplitudes as the stimulation frequency

Supplementary Fig. 17, the photoresponse ion current variations were measured as a
function of KCl electrolyte with concentrations from 0.1mM to 100 mM. A significant
negative baseline drift was observed exclusively in the 100 mM KCl solution. We
attribute this phenomenon to the following potential causes:
(1) Interfacial polarization effects: In high-concentration KCl solutions, the elevated

2
in a negative shift of the measurement baseline.
Although ion concentration influences the initial current baseline drift, the current
stabilizes at a baseline level after a sufficient equilibration period. To clearly illustrate
the effect of ion concentration on the change in photocurrent, specifically, the absolute
difference between illuminated and dark conditions, in the revised supplementary
information of updated Supplementary Fig. 17, the data were zero-referenced (baseline-
subtracted) for enhanced comparability.

## Paper

## Abstract

Biological vision acquires externTal information through light-induced transmembrane ion transport, generating
electrical impulses. Emulating the dual visual functions of photoreceptors and photosynapses through light-
modulated ion transport presents a significant challenge. Herein, we present a bioinspired light-regulated
nanofluidic iontronic device that can mimic biological visual functionalities, realized through an engineered
carbon nanotube and molybdenum disulfide (CNT/MoS ) heterostructure. This bioinspired device combines two
2
key functionalities of photoreceptor-like optical sensing and photosynaptic signal processing with dynamically
adjustable polarity-switching behavior, achieved via bias voltage–modulated transient photoresponse speeds.
Both theoretical and experimental results prove that light-modulated ion transport originates from the
heterointerface-induced asymmetric photovoltage generation across CNT/MoS nanotube. Furthermore, we
2
demonstrate its implementation for both accurate orientation recognition and reliable fingerprint detection under
varying incident light angles. The device's bidirectional photoresponsiveness highlights its unique advantages
for adaptive visual simulation systems.

---

## Introduction

In biological systems, approximately 80% of external information is processed primarily through the visual
system1. The retina, a sophisticated neural tissue lining the posterior eye, serves as the gateway for visual
perception, owing to its anatomically integrated and intricately organized structure2 (Fig. 1a). Among these, the
photoreceptor cells and photosynaptic layers serve as the most critical components, with the former specializing
in light reception and the latter mediating information storage and interlayer communication3. Photoreceptor
cells rapidly capture light stimuli and convert them into electrical signals via photosensitive protein channel,
which precisely regulate ion transport, inducing membrane hyperpolarizaStion4 (Fig. 1b). The resulting light-
dependent electrical signals propagate via synaptic connections to downstream retinal neurons, enabling visual
information processing5 (Fig. 1c). Inspired by biological vision Rsystems, researchers have developed solid-state
optoelectronic devices that leverage semiconductor-based electron-hole separation mechanisms to emulate both
photoreceptor sensing and synaptic preprocessing functions6-11. However, the mechanisms behind how light
triggers localized interactions between electroEns, holes, and ions at interfaces are still not fully understood. This
gap in knowledge limits our ability to accurately mimic the ion-mediated signal transmission found in biological
visual systems, slowing the developmIent of advanced artificial photoreceptors and photosynaptic devices.
Over the past five years, Radvances in nanofluidic memristors have exploited nonlinear ion transport through
spatially confined systems in nano- and sub-nano channels and membranes to emulate biological synaptic
information processing, enabling brain-like computation through electrical-to-ionic and ionic-to-electrical signal
transduction mechanisms12-16. Meanwhile, recent advances in optically controlled ion transport based on ion-
conductive hydrogels and nanofluidic channel materials have partially achieved bioinspired visual
functionalities17,18. However, current research primarily focuses on biological photosynaptic functions, which
are limited by slow light-response speeds, thus failing to replicate the rapid detection of high-frequency visual
signals characteristic of photoreceptors. Given these limitations, creating a bioinspired visual system within a
single nanofluidic device that integrates photoreceptor-like optical sensing, photosynaptic processing, and
polarity-switching is still a major challenge.
Herein, we present a light-controlled nanofluidic iontronic device based on a carbon nanotube and
molybdenum disulfide (CNT/MoS ) heterostructure that emulates biological visual functions through a
2
sequential “light stimuli-electrical signal-electron/ion coupling-ionic signal” transduction process (Fig. 1d). This
platform achieves dual photoreceptor- and photosynaptic-like functionalities within a single device via bias-
voltage-controlled modulation of photoresponse dynamics. In a two-terminal model without bias voltage, the
device replicates photoreceptor cell operations with a rapid photocurrent responsive speed and responsive
specificity of light power density and wavelength. In a three-terminal configuration with bias voltage, the device
demonstrates photosynaptic characteristics including short-term plasticity, long-term plasticity, and experience-
dependent learning behaviors. The mechanism arises from the coupled effect between bias voltage and
photogenerated potential (E ) across the heterostructure nanotube (Fig. 1d), which together precisely control
photo S
ion transport across the CNT/MoS nanotube. This is facilitated by thSe one-dimensional coaxial architecture,
2
which establishes a continuous and enlarged heterointerface that not only enhances photogenerated charge
separation and strengthens the built-in electric field, but alsoP gives rise to a heterointerface-induced asymmetric
photovoltage. This photovoltage directly drives ioNn transport in a manner distinct from conventional
photothermal or surface-charge modulation sch emes19-21. The resulting ion photocurrent reaches 526 nA,
exceeding the performance of state-of-theL-art nanofluidic opto-ionic systems based on established material
platforms like metal organic framework (MOF)17, covalent organic frameworks (COFs)22, two-dimensional
transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes)19, and layered graphene oxide (GO)23,24. Furthermore, this
iontronic device realizes aAccurate orientation recognition and robust fingerprint detection across a wide range of
incident light angles, highlighting its potential for biointerfaced artificial retina.

Fabrication and Characterization of Nanotubes Heterostructure

The CNTs were synthesized through a CVD equipment (BTF-1200 C-Ⅱ, AnHui BEQ Equipment Technology

2
